skill.name: Sound devices: alliteration, onomatopoeia, rhythm and rhyme
skill.why: How words sound together makes writing fun to hear and easy to remember.
skill.how: Read it aloud. Listen for repeated starts, noisy words, rhymes and a steady beat.

encounters.frame: Poet Pip read this poem to the crew while a storm rolled across the bay.
encounters.text:
STORM ON THE BAY

Dark clouds gather over the bay.
The pelicans hide among the trees.
The fishing boats are tied up tight.
A cold wind tugs at our sleeves.

Then, far away, a flash of white.
The thunder booms across the water.
The rain arrives in heavy sheets.
The jetty shines like melted butter.

We watch it all from the cabin door,
with Mo's hot chocolate in our hands.
By morning, the storm has moved away,
and crabs are back out on the sands.

encounters.text:
Zed wrote this poem after watching a rocket launch on the big screen at school. He read it at assembly, and the whole school joined in with the countdown.

LAUNCH DAY

Silver stars shine overhead.
The crew is up and out of bed.
Ten, nine, eight, the countdown's on.
Seven, six, and then it's gone!
Whoosh! The rocket leaves the ground.
It shakes the boardwalk all around.
It's heading out to reach the moon.
We hope it gets there very soon.

Afterwards, Tully said it was the best poem ever read at assembly. Zed pointed out that it was the only poem ever read at assembly. Then he wrote a note about the sound devices he had used.

encounters.frame: Gus wrote a chant for his robot. The Plonkett is marching along to it.
encounters.text:
Gus built a robot out of tins, springs and an old toaster. To test it, he wrote a chant and read it out while the robot marched up and down the deck.

ROBOT MARCH

Clank, clank, march.
Clank, clank, march.
Left foot, right foot.
Clank, clank, march.

Bolts are tight.
Gears are greased.
Clank, clank, march.
Off it goes!

Clank, clank, march.
Clank, clank, march.
Down the deck and back again.
Clank, clank, stop.

The robot really did march down the deck and back again. Then it stopped, right on the last line, and Gus took a bow. The crew clapped. The Plonkett tried to march too, but it mostly hopped.

encounters.text:
Indi spent all of Saturday painting a mural on the old boatshed. She painted pelicans, mudskippers and a Plonkett with a banjo. It took six cans of paint and two very long brushes, and she got paint in her hair, on her thongs and on the Plonkett. When she finished, she wrote a poem about it for the noticeboard.

THE MURAL

I took my brushes to the shore.
I took my paints, and then some more.
I painted crabs and frogs so small,
and herons, thin and very tall,
across the boatshed's big brown ___.

Indi chewed the end of her brush. The last word had to rhyme, and it had to make sense too.

encounters.frame: Tully wrote a poem about the swimming carnival for the school newsletter.
encounters.text:
Tully wrote this poem about the Year 5 and 6 relay at the island swimming carnival. She read it aloud at the presentation night, and the whole relay team stood up and bowed.

THE RELAY

The whistle blows. The race is on.
Our keen coach calls out to Kai.
Splash! Each arm dives into the pool.
Cheering crowds circle the stands.

Hear them cheer, both far and near.
The parents stand. The teachers yell.
The last swimmer turns, and kicks, and pushes.
Ruby wins it, half a metre in front.

The ribbons come, the photos flash,
and everybody's soaking wet.
The relay team all hug and jump,
the best race that we've seen yet.

Afterwards, Ms Ali asked Tully which line she was proudest of. Tully said the ending, because it had taken her a whole week to get it sounding right.

encounters.frame: Poet Pip wrote a poem after her dive on the reef. The Plonkett can't swim that deep, so it stayed in the boat.
encounters.text:
REEF DIVE
by Poet Pip

We roll backwards off the boat,
into a world of green and blue.
The chain clanks against the hull.
Then everything goes quiet.
Pale coral, chalky white and cinnamon brown,
stretches out beneath us.

Bright blue butterflyfish bob below.
Kelp curls and coils in the current.
We float above the coral bed.
A turtle bumps me on the head.

An octopus peers out of a crack,
then squeezes in and won't come back.
Our air runs low, it's time to rise.
We climb aboard with salty eyes.

Poet Pip says she wrote the poem on the boat ride home, with a wet towel round her shoulders, and she read it out loud to herself again and again. 'A poem isn't finished,' she says, 'until it sounds right in your mouth.' She changed one line six times before she was happy with it.

encounters.text:
Every footy club has a song, and Tully thinks the Reef Rays song is the best one in the league. The players sing it in the rooms after every win, and the fans sing it in the stands, usually much too loudly. This week, she decided the whole crew had to learn it before the grand final. She made everyone stand on the deck in a line and sing it six times.

THE REEF RAYS SONG

We are the Rays, the Reef Rays!
We play it hard, we play it fair.
We fly so high we touch the sky,
we kick it long and through the air.
So clap your hands and stamp your feet,
the Reef Rays never know defeat!

By the sixth time, Mo knew all the words, Zed was conducting with a spoon, and the Plonkett was croaking along on every beat.

encounters.frame: Zed found this poem scratched into the wall of an old hut in the mangroves. The Plonkett won't go back there.
encounters.text:
THE HUT AT THE END OF THE BOARDWALK

I pushed the door. It gave a creak.
I stepped inside. I couldn't speak.
The room was black. My torch was dead.
Something dripped above my head.

Drip. Drip. Drip. Then all was still.
A cold wind blew across the sill.
The floorboards groaned beneath my feet.
Then came a thud. My heart skipped a beat.

I didn't wait to find out who.
I ran so fast I lost a shoe.
And if you walk that way at night,
you'd better bring a brighter light.

Nobody knows who wrote the poem. Zed copied it into his notebook and read it to the crew by torchlight. When he got to the thud, Gus dropped his hot chocolate, and Mo said he would be sleeping with the cabin light on.

encounters.frame: Indi wrote a poem about Mo's cooking. The Plonkett ate the last word.
encounters.text:
Indi wrote this poem for the galley noticeboard, after Mo tried a new recipe: a meat pie filled with sardines, custard and a whole tin of baked beans. Mo was very proud of it. He served it to Gus first, because Gus will usually eat anything.

MO'S SPECIAL PIE

Mo made a pie and served it hot.
He'd used up everything he'd got.
The crust was thick, the top was brown.
Gus took a bite and wore a ___.

He chewed it once. He chewed it twice.
He said, 'Well, Mo, that's very... nice.'
Then Mo went off to make some tea,
and Gus fed the Plonkett, quick as can be.

Mo found out the next morning, when the Plonkett followed him around the deck all day, hoping for seconds.

encounters.frame: Poet Pip, Keeper of Mirage Mangroves, has written a poem about the island at dawn. She wants to know if you can hear what she did.
encounters.text:
Poet Pip writes a poem every morning before anyone else on the island is awake. She sits at the end of the boardwalk with a notebook and a thermos, waits for the mist to arrive, and reads every line aloud to the mangroves until it sounds exactly right. This is the one she pinned to the noticeboard this week.

MIRAGE AT DAWN

Before the sun, before the birds,
before the boats begin to stir,
soft, silent, silver, the mist slides in
and wraps the mangroves, root and limb.

It settles slowly on the tide.
It hides the jetty, hides the shore.
The island holds its breath and waits,
as still as it has been before.

Then light: a crack of gold, a gull,
a fisherman who starts his motor.
The mist lifts up and drifts away,
and morning floods across the water.

Pip says the first stanza is the hardest to get right. 'The mist never makes a sound,' she says. 'It creeps in so softly that you only notice it when the jetty has gone.'

encounters.success: The soft, repeated s sounds are hushed, like the quiet mist creeping in. Pip says the mist makes no sound.

options.text: It makes the line sound sharp and loud, like a warning.
options.reason: Pip says the mist never makes a sound. Would a sharp, loud line match it?

options.text: It makes the line rhyme with the line that comes before it.
options.reason: Rhyme is when word endings sound the same, like night and bright. These words share their first sound instead.

encounters.frame: Wren wrote a poem about the wetland at dusk. Then she tried changing five lines.
encounters.text:
Wren doesn't usually write poems. She says she prefers animals to words, because animals never argue about commas. But after a whole evening sitting by the lagoon on the far side of Mirage Mangroves, she had counted eleven different animal sounds in one hour. She tried to fit as many as she could into a poem, and wrote it down in the back of her field notebook and showed it to Poet Pip.

THE LAGOON AT DUSK

The sun goes down behind the trees.
The water turns to copper glass.
Two black swans glide across the bay.
The reeds bow down to let them pass.

Then everything begins to sing.
The frogs go plonk. The crickets chirp.
A pelican lands with a splash,
and gulps a fish, and gives a burp.

The mosquitoes muster in the murk.
The bats wake up inside their camp.
The stars appear, the moon is high,
the whole lagoon grows cool and damp.

Poet Pip read it twice. Then she said it was the first poem she had ever read that made her want to put on insect spray. Wren took that as a compliment. Then she asked if she could put it on the island's welcome sign.

encounters.frame: Tully wrote a poem about the island fun run. The Plonkett came last, but it did finish.
encounters.text:
Every year, the whole of Mirage Mangroves runs the five-kilometre fun run along the boardwalk and back. This year more than three hundred people took part, including two dogs and a man dressed as a mudskipper. Tully has won the Under 12s three years in a row, and this year she wrote a poem about it for the school newsletter. She told the editor that the shape of the poem was meant to match the shape of the race.

THE FUN RUN

We gather at the starting line, a crowd of sleepy, yawning faces,
with sunscreen on our noses and our runners double-laced.
The hooter sounds, and off we go, a slow and happy shuffle,
past the mangroves and the mudflats and the ranger's little hut.

By halfway, all the chatter stops. We puff along the boardwalk.
The sun is hot. My legs are lead. I see the finish flags.

Faster now.
Faster still.
Pound the boards.
Pass the pack.
Arms pump.
Heart thumps.
One more step.
Done!

She came second this year, by about the length of a footy. She says the poem is still a winner. Next year she wants to write about the swimming carnival, which she says will need much wetter words. Gus has offered to time her with a stopwatch he built out of an old egg timer.

encounters.frame: Zed wrote a theme song for his game Swamp Quest, and a note on what its sounds do. Tully spotted a mistake.
encounters.text:
Zed has been building his game, Swamp Quest, for most of the term. The hero is a Plonkett who has to rescue Creatures from a gold castle in the middle of the swamp. The castle is guarded by goblins, rolling barrels and a very grumpy robot crocodile. The game needed a theme song, so Zed wrote one, and Mo, Gus and Indi recorded it on the deck using a bucket, two spoons and a ukulele with only three strings. It took them nine tries to get through it without Mo laughing, and the Plonkett joined in on the chorus.

SWAMP QUEST THEME

Beat the boss and bag the bonus!
Jump the gaps and dodge the darts!
Whack! Thud! The goblin's down.
Now grab the key and save the hearts!

We hop by day, we fight by night.
We never stop, we never quit.
The castle's gold, the castle's tall,
but one small frog can conquer it.

Zed wanted the song to sound like a fight you could win. He then wrote a note for the help screen, explaining what his sound devices do, because he says every good game has a help screen that nobody reads. Tully read it. She found one mistake. Zed says he will fix it in the next update, which could be any time between tomorrow and Year 7.

encounters.frame: A crackly message has reached the Soggy Biscuit's radio. Zed wrote it down, word for word.
encounters.text:
Zed was on night watch when the old radio in the wheelhouse came to life. It was the island's amateur radio club, who had been trying for weeks to talk to the space station as it passed overhead. They had finally done it, and they were reading out the astronaut's reply for anyone listening. Zed grabbed a pencil and wrote down everything he heard.

'This is the station, passing over the southern islands. Down below, I can see the lights of your towns scattered like spilled glitter. The sea is black. There's a storm out to the east, flashing on and off. Up here it's so quiet that I can hear my own heartbeat. Thank you, Mirage Mangroves. Your signal is coming through clear. We'll pass over you again tomorrow, at the same time.'

Then the line Zed underlined twice in his notebook:

The radio crackles, then hisses into silence.

He sat there in the dark for a long time after that, looking up, wondering which of the moving lights was the station. In the morning he told the crew, and Tully worked out exactly when it would come over again.

encounters.success: Crackles and hisses let you hear the signal fade. Then silence, and Zed sits alone in the dark, looking up.
